newsitem.title: JAPAN: Gulf conflict casts shadow on Okinawa bases vote.
newsitem.headline: Gulf conflict casts shadow on Okinawa bases vote.

text.p: The latest United States attack against Iraq has cast a long shadow over Japan's southern island of Okinawa, where islanders vote on Sunday in the country's first referendum on U.S. military bases.

The expected vote in favour of "streamlining" U.S. bases will boost Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota in his efforts to win a phased withdrawal of U.S. forces from his remote prefecture, which is Japan's poorest.
Since a rape case last year involving U.S. servicemen, bases on Okinawa have become a thorny issue for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's coalition government.

Several Japanese newspapers on Friday said Hashimoto was considering calling snap elections next month, although he has denied the reports, citing uncertainty over the result of the Okinawa referendum.

Although U.S. military units stationed in Okinawa did not take part in attacks against Iraq this week, anti-bases activists in Okinawa say such military action puts the spotlight again on the strategic importance of bases here.
One U.S. ship stationed in Japan was reportedly involved in the Iraq operation, sparking criticism from activists.

"U.S. leaders probably thought twice before sending Okinawa-based units to Iraq this time, because a move like that might affect the result of Sunday's referendum," said Yoshimasa Karimata, vice president of the Okinawa Prefectural Resident's Referendum Promotion Council, an umbrella organisation of trade unions, anti-bases and citizens' groups.
"The attack underscored the importance of these bases for the U.S. military, which we don't want," Karimata said.
B-52 bombers from Guam took part in the first wave of missile attacks last Tuesday but did not refuel on Okinawa.

The referendum comes on the heels of a decision by Japan's Supreme Court on August 28 which ruled against Okinawa Governor Ota, who had refused to sign documents to allow the forced appropriation of private land for U.S. bases.

The Supreme Court threw out Ota's claims that the concentration of U.S. bases in Okinawa violated the constitution. Okinawa houses more than 75 percent of U.S. military facilities and half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan, including an entire Marine Corps division.
The non-binding referendum is a "yes" or "no" vote on the question: "Do you support reviewing the U.S.-Japan Status of Forces Agreement and streamlining U.S. bases in the prefecture?"
It is not directly linked to Governor Ota's plan to seek a phased withdrawal of all U.S. bases in Okinawa by 2015.

The only groups campaigning for the "no" vote are a handful of ultra-nationalists, and the result is not in doubt. The key is the turnout and the percentage of the "yes" vote, Karimata and other officials said.
Okinawa newspaper Ryukyu Shimpo said on Friday its poll of 300 people showed 76 percent of 900,000 eligible voters would take part and 80 percent would cast "yes" ballots.

The Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), which governs the legal standing of U.S. military personnel, became the focus of public outcry last September after U.S. military authorities delayed handing over to Japanese police three U.S. servicemen later convicted of raping a 12-year old Okinawan schoolgirl.

The rape case triggered public anger against the Japanese government for having done nothing to lessen the burden of hosting huge U.S. bases on Okinawa, which for the U.S. military is a strategic outpost in the western Pacific.
